title: Fork
body: One piece attacks two or more targets at once. Check whether one target can move with check or create a stronger threat before assuming the fork wins material.

title: Pin
body: Moving a pinned piece exposes a more valuable target behind it. An absolute pin exposes the king and makes such a move illegal; a relative pin may be ignored tactically.

title: Skewer
body: A valuable front piece is attacked along a line; when it moves, a target behind it is lost. Unlike a pin, the more valuable piece stands in front.

title: Discovered attack
body: A moving piece uncovers an attack by a bishop, rook or queen behind it. The moving piece may create a second threat at the same time.

title: Double check
body: Both the moving piece and an uncovered piece give check. Capturing or blocking only one attacker does not answer both checks, so a legal reply must move the king.

title: Deflection
body: A defender is lured away from an important square or duty. Identify what becomes undefended after the forced response.

title: Attraction
body: A piece is drawn onto a particular square where a second tactic works. Deflection emphasizes leaving a duty; attraction emphasizes the destination.

title: Overloading
body: One defender has more tasks than it can maintain. Force it to perform one duty, then exploit the task it abandons.

title: Interference
body: A move blocks an enemy line of defense or attack. Sacrificing on the crossing point of two defensive lines can create two different winning responses.

title: Novotny
body: A sacrifice on the intersection of two differently moving line pieces creates interference whichever piece captures. It is a classic problem theme that can also occur in games.

title: Grimshaw
body: Two defending line pieces interfere with one another on the same square in different variations, without an initial sacrifice on that square. It is most often seen in composed problems.

title: Plachutta
body: A sacrifice creates mutual interference between two similarly moving line pieces. Because either piece can capture, their duties must be carefully separated by the follow-up.

title: Clearance
body: A square or line is vacated so another piece can use it. The clearing move may be a sacrifice, a check, or a quiet move that gains time.

title: Zwischenzug
body: An in-between move interrupts an expected sequence, often a recapture. Forcing checks and threats can change the material balance before normal play resumes.

title: Desperado
body: A piece that will be lost anyway captures or creates a threat before disappearing. Its final action extracts value from an otherwise doomed position.

title: Windmill
body: A repeated discovered-check mechanism lets an attacking piece collect material between checks. The defending king is forced back to a square that permits the next cycle.

title: X-ray attack
body: A line piece influences a target through an intervening piece that may move or be exchanged. X-ray defense can make an apparently loose piece tactically safe.

title: Undermining
body: The supporting pawn or piece beneath a target is attacked. Capturing the support can make the main target collapse even when it has several direct defenders.

title: Back-rank mate
body: A rook or queen mates a king confined by its own pawns or pieces on the back rank. Giving the king luft can help, but only if the escape square is actually safe.

title: Smothered mate
body: A knight mates a king whose own pieces occupy all escape squares. A queen sacrifice often forces the final blocking piece into place.

title: Arabian mate
body: A rook and knight coordinate against a king near a corner. The knight protects the rook and covers a key escape square.

title: Anastasia’s mate
body: A rook or queen checks along an edge while a knight seals escape squares, often with an enemy pawn blocking the remaining route. The name comes from an early nineteenth-century novel.

title: Boden’s mate
body: Two bishops on crossing diagonals mate a king trapped by its own pieces, often after queenside castling. A sacrifice can open the decisive diagonal.

title: Greek gift
body: A bishop sacrifice on h7 or h2 draws the king out so a knight and queen can attack. It is sound only if the attacking pieces can arrive and the king cannot safely escape.

title: Legal’s mate
body: A pinned knight moves to allow a queen capture, while minor pieces force mate. The pattern works only when the defender actually accepts the poisoned queen.

title: Epaulette mate
body: A queen mates a king whose two sideways escape squares are blocked by its own pieces. The blocking pieces resemble shoulder decorations.

title: Dovetail mate
body: A queen checks a diagonally adjacent king while friendly pieces block the king’s rear diagonal escapes. The queen itself must be protected.

title: Swallow’s-tail mate
body: The checking queen stands immediately beside the king, and the king’s pieces block diagonal retreats on the other side. Exact geometry distinguishes it from the dovetail.

title: Underpromotion
body: A pawn promotes to a rook, bishop or knight rather than a queen. Reasons include avoiding stalemate, giving a knight fork, or delivering a specific mate.

title: Perpetual check
body: One side can keep giving checks that the opponent cannot escape without unacceptable loss. The actual draw follows repetition or another rule, rather than a separate perpetual-check rule.

title: Domination
body: One piece controls all useful destinations of an opposing piece. A trapped knight or bishop may be lost without being directly attacked yet.

title: Quiet move
body: A move that is neither check nor capture can make an unavoidable threat. Candidate-move calculation must include quiet moves when forcing checks fail.

title: Cross-check
body: A check is answered by blocking it with a piece that itself gives check. The idea appears in tactical games and composed problems.

title: Battery
body: Two coordinated line pieces share a file, rank or diagonal. The front piece can move to uncover the rear attacker, or one piece can support the other’s entry.

title: Rundlauf
body: A piece travels a circuit and returns to its starting square, while the position has changed in a useful way. The theme is especially common in chess composition.

title: Switchback
body: A piece moves to a square and later returns to its original square, often after forcing a weakening response. The return is purposeful rather than simply lost time.

title: Excelsior
body: A pawn travels from its starting rank to promotion during a composed solution. The named theme originated in a problem by Sam Loyd.

title: Babson task
body: A direct-mate composition answers each of Black’s four promotion choices with the corresponding White promotion. Leonid Yarosh’s 1983 orthodox setting was a landmark.

title: Allumwandlung
body: A composed solution or its variations feature all four promotion types. It need not have the matching-response structure of a Babson task.

title: Hole
body: A weak square cannot be defended by an appropriate pawn because those pawns have advanced, disappeared or become fixed. A hole matters most when an enemy piece can occupy it securely.

title: Outpost
body: A secure advanced square supports a piece, often a knight, without easy challenge by enemy pawns. A square is less useful if the piece has no targets from it.

title: Prophylaxis
body: Anticipate the opponent’s useful plan and limit it while improving your position. It is not simply passive defense: the best prophylactic moves often serve two purposes.

title: Minority attack
body: Fewer pawns advance against a larger pawn group to create a fixed weakness, commonly b4–b5 against c6 in the Carlsbad structure. The aim is a target, not necessarily a passed pawn.

title: Isolated queen’s pawn
body: An isolated d-pawn has no adjacent friendly pawn to support it. Its owner gets space and active pieces; a blockade and exchanges favor the defender.

title: Hanging pawns
body: Adjacent pawns on open neighboring files, often c4 and d4, support each other but cannot be defended by other pawns. Their strength depends on activity and well-timed advances.

title: Backward pawn
body: A pawn lags behind neighboring pawns and cannot safely advance. It is especially vulnerable on an open or semi-open file.

title: Good bishop / bad bishop
body: A bishop blocked by its own fixed pawns is conventionally “bad,” but it may still defend important squares. Judge activity and useful targets, not only pawn colors.

title: Color complex
body: A network of squares of one color can become weak after pawn moves or a bishop exchange. An attack may exploit that network without targeting a single fixed square.

title: Exchange sacrifice
body: A rook is given for a bishop or knight to gain positional or tactical compensation. Typical returns include a permanent outpost, damaged pawns, or a dangerous king attack.

title: Blockade
body: A piece occupies a square directly in front of an enemy pawn, preventing its advance. Knights are often effective blockaders because they attack beyond the blocked pawn.

title: Space advantage
body: Advanced pawns control territory and restrict the opponent’s maneuvering. The cramped side often seeks exchanges or a freeing pawn break.

title: Pawn break
body: A pawn move challenges an opposing pawn chain and changes the available files or diagonals. Preparation matters because the resulting structure may favor either side.

title: Candidate passed pawn
body: A pawn may become passed after a favorable exchange or breakthrough. It is a potential resource, unlike a pawn that is already free of opposing pawns ahead on adjacent files.

title: Outside passed pawn
body: A passed pawn far from the main pawn mass can distract the enemy king. Its value depends on whether the other side gains a more dangerous central passer or attack.

title: Initiative
body: One side makes threats that force the opponent to respond, controlling the direction of play. The initiative can disappear if a threat is harmless or a defender finds a counterattack.

title: Compensation
body: Material loss is balanced by activity, king exposure, space or structural gains. Compensation can be temporary; identify whether it must become a concrete result.

title: Principle of two weaknesses
body: A defender may hold one target but struggle when a second target is created far away. Switching play can overload a tied-down defense.

title: Transformation of advantage
body: A temporary edge can be converted into a different lasting asset, such as exchanging an attack for a favorable endgame. Keeping the original advantage forever is not always possible.

title: Rook lift
body: A rook develops along a rank before moving to another file, often joining a kingside attack through the third rank. Check the central squares it must cross.

title: Opposition
body: Kings separated by one square contest entry squares. Direct opposition is only one tool: distant opposition, pawn moves and the position of the board edges can change the result.

title: Triangulation
body: A king or other piece takes a three-move route to return to a useful position with the opponent to move. The aim is to transfer the move without losing the position.

title: Corresponding squares
body: Pairs of squares dictate where a defender must stand to answer an attacking king. Opposition is a simple special case; more complex pawn endgames require a wider map.

title: Lucena position
body: A rook and pawn on the seventh rank can win by building a bridge against checking attacks. The attacking rook shields its king so the pawn can promote.

title: Philidor position
body: The defending rook holds the third rank while the enemy pawn remains behind it, then switches to rear checks after the pawn advances. Exact king and pawn placement matter.

title: Vancura defense
body: Against a rook pawn, a defending rook can attack the pawn from the side while keeping checking distance. The defending king must avoid being forced away from the corner.

title: Short-side defense
body: In rook endings, the defending king often belongs on the short side of the pawn, leaving the rook room to check from the long side. Too little checking distance can lose.

title: Fortress
body: The weaker side builds a position the stronger side cannot penetrate despite a material advantage. A claimed fortress must survive waiting moves, pawn breaks and zugzwang.

title: Zugzwang
body: Every legal move worsens the position, so having the turn is harmful. It is common in king-and-pawn endings but also occurs with many pieces.

title: Trebuchet
body: A reciprocal-zugzwang king-and-pawn position: each king protects its own pawn while attacking the opponent’s. Whoever moves must give ground.

title: Rook behind the passer
body: A rook behind a passed pawn usually gains scope as the pawn advances. This is a useful guideline, not a rule: immediate tactics and checking geometry can override it.

title: Shouldering
body: A king uses its body to prevent the enemy king from approaching along the shortest route. The maneuver can gain a decisive tempo in a pawn race.

title: Tablebase
body: An exact database classifies supported low-material positions under specified rules. Distance-to-mate and distance-to-zeroing measure different things, and move-count rules can change a practical result.

title: Saavedra position
body: A famous pawn study wins through rook underpromotion to avoid stalemate. Promoting to the strongest piece would throw away the win.

title: Réti study
body: A king simultaneously approaches a hostile passer and supports its own pawn. Diagonal movement lets it pursue two goals without losing as much time as a straight-line chase.

title: En passant
body: Immediately after a pawn advances two squares, an opposing pawn beside it may capture it as if it had advanced one. The capture is illegal if it exposes the capturing side’s king.

title: Castling
body: The king moves two squares toward a rook, which crosses to the square beside it. Neither piece may have moved; the king cannot be in check, cross check, or finish in check.

title: Threefold repetition
body: A player can claim a draw when the same position occurs three times with the same side to move and the same legal possibilities. Castling and en-passant rights can make similar-looking positions different.

title: Fifty-move rule
body: A player can claim a draw after fifty moves by each side without a pawn move or capture. The automatic seventy-five-move rule is a separate limit; checkmate on the last move takes precedence.

title: Swiss tournament
body: Players with similar scores are paired over a fixed number of rounds without a complete round-robin. Pairing constraints and tie-breaks influence final standings.

title: Round-robin tournament
body: Every participant plays every other participant, once or multiple times. A double round-robin gives each player both colors against each opponent.

title: Candidates tournament
body: The challenger-selection event in the modern world-championship cycle. Formats have varied across history, including matches and round-robin tournaments.

title: Elo rating
body: A relative estimate of playing strength updated from results and expected scores. A higher rating is not a guarantee of winning an individual game.

title: FIDE
body: The international chess federation organizes championships and maintains international ratings and titles. Federation ratings differ from online-site ratings.

title: US Chess
body: The United States federation maintains its own ratings and member records. Its rating pool and rules are distinct from FIDE’s, so the numbers are not directly interchangeable.

title: Grandmaster
body: A FIDE title usually earned through rating and norm requirements, with exceptions for designated events. It is a title, not a temporary rating category.

title: PGN
body: Portable Game Notation stores game headers and algebraic move text, with optional comments and variations. It describes a game score rather than just a single board position.

title: FEN
body: Forsyth–Edwards Notation describes piece placement, side to move, castling rights, en-passant square and move counters. Two positions with identical pieces can have different legal moves.

title: Chess960
body: A randomized starting arrangement keeps bishops on opposite colors and the king between the rooks. Castling ends with the same king and rook destinations as in standard chess.

title: Touch-move
body: In over-the-board play, deliberately touching a movable own piece normally commits the player to move it. Announcing an adjustment before touching distinguishes correcting a piece’s placement.

title: Italian Game
body: Build d4 without rushing it. The c4 bishop points at f7, but a prepared center break is usually more useful than a one-piece attack. c3 supports d4; d3 keeps the center stable until the pieces are ready.

title: Ruy Lopez
body: Pressure e5 indirectly. White often preserves the bishop and builds a center while Black gains queenside space. A closed center gives both sides time to maneuver; opening it changes which pieces are strong.

title: Queen's Gambit Declined
body: Use pressure on d5 to choose a favorable pawn structure. Black is solid but must solve the c8 bishop. After cxd5 exd5, White’s queenside minority can target c6; keeping central tension leaves more options.

title: Queen's Gambit Accepted
body: Black gives up the center temporarily for development and a later ...c5 break. Holding c4 at all costs is unnecessary. White’s d4–e4 center gains space, but can become a target after exchanges.

title: Sicilian Defense
body: The c-pawn exchange gives Black a semi-open c-file and a central pawn majority. White gets quick development and space. White’s d-pawn has disappeared; the d5 square can become an outpost if Black plays ...e5.

title: Caro-Kann Defense
body: Black develops the light-squared bishop before ...e6. White’s space is useful only if it becomes activity. The c6 pawn supports d5; ...c5 challenges the center later but costs a second c-pawn move.

title: French Defense
body: Attack the base of the pawn chain, not just its head. Black pressures d4; White often uses the kingside space. The locked e5–d4 versus e6–d5 chains direct attacks to opposite wings.

title: Nimzo-Indian Defense
body: Black trades a bishop to slow e4 and influence the center. White chooses between clean pawns and faster development. Bxc3 can double White’s c-pawns; Qc2 avoids that but spends a queen tempo.

title: King's Indian Defense
body: White owns central space; Black accepts less room to seek a kingside pawn break. Speed matters when attacks run on opposite wings. Once d5 locks the center, White tends toward c5 and Black toward ...f5–f4.

title: Grünfeld Defense
body: Black invites a broad center, then attacks it from a distance. White’s task is to make the center mobile before it becomes a target. The c3 pawn becomes d4’s support after bxc3; exchanges can leave an isolated central pawn.

title: Catalan Opening
body: The g2 bishop creates long-term queenside pressure. White can recover c4 without rushing if development compensates. The long diagonal matters most when the center opens; a closed d5 pawn can blunt the bishop.

title: Slav Defense
body: Black keeps the light-squared bishop free before ...e6. White often plays a4 to stop ...b5 from holding c4. The c6–d5 chain is solid, but c6 can become a target if Black falls behind.

title: Semi-Slav Defense
body: Black combines a solid triangle with a prepared ...c5 break. White can use the center before Black’s queenside develops fully. After ...dxc4 and ...b5, the c8 bishop finds b7 and Black hits the center with ...c5.

title: English Opening
body: Use c4 to control d5 and choose a central structure later. The first move does not commit White to a single pawn formation. A Botvinnik structure with c4–d3–e4 grips d5 but leaves d4 as a square to watch.

title: Scotch Game
body: Open the center early and develop with tempo. The d4 knight is active but can become a target. With both central d-pawns exchanged or challenged, piece activity matters more than a closed pawn chain.

title: London System
body: Develop the bishop before closing the e-pawn chain, but adapt to Black’s central and queenside pressure. The d4–e3–c3 triangle supports e5 and keeps the center stable.

title: Scandinavian Defense
body: Black trades the d-pawn and develops the queen early. White gains time by attacking it while developing. The c6–e6 structure supports d5; White has more space but must turn it into active pieces.

title: Modern Defense
body: Black delays the king’s knight and invites a broad center. Flexibility is valuable only if the center is challenged in time. White has a d4–e4 center; Black’s ...c5 or ...e5 break determines the middlegame.

title: Dutch Defense
body: Black uses ...f5 to control e4, accepting a king-side weakness. Stonewall and fluid-center structures require different plans. In a Stonewall, the d5–e6–f5 chain grips e4 but leaves e5 weak.

title: Alekhine Defense
body: Black provokes advancing pawns and then attacks them. White must avoid confusing space with secure control. An e5 pawn gains a tempo against the knight but can become a target of ...d6.

title: Petrov's Defense
body: Black counterattacks e4 instead of immediately defending e5. Accurate timing prevents a tactical loss in the center. Early central exchanges often lead to symmetrical pawns, but open files reward the better-developed side.

title: Vienna Game
body: White keeps the f-pawn free by developing Nc3 first. A later f4 must be timed against Black’s central counterplay. The e4 pawn can be reinforced with d3 or paired with d4; f4 changes king safety.

title: Four Knights Game
body: Fast symmetrical development brings both sides close to castling. The first central break decides the structure. The center can become open after d4 or stay restrained with d3.

title: Tarrasch Defense
body: Black accepts an isolated d-pawn in exchange for active bishops and central space. Exchanges can change the balance. The isolated d5 pawn controls c4 and e4 but cannot be defended by another pawn.

title: King's Gambit Accepted
body: White gives a pawn for rapid development and open lines. Black can return material to complete development safely. The f-file opens for White, but f2 no longer shields the king.

title: Queen's Indian Defense
body: Black controls e4 with pieces and the b7 bishop rather than an early central occupation. White tries to make that bishop ineffective. A d4–c4 center can be challenged by ...d5 or ...c5; e3 changes the g1 knight’s options.

title: Bogo-Indian Defense
body: The early ...Bb4+ makes White choose a block before Black commits the center. The bishop may trade or retreat. The structure depends on whether White blocks with Bd2, Nd2 or Nc3.

title: Benoni Defense
body: Black concedes a space advantage to create asymmetric counterplay. The d6 pawn is a weakness, while the queenside majority can move. White has d5 and e4 against Black’s d6 and c5; the g7 bishop pressures the queenside.

title: Benko Gambit Accepted
body: Black sacrifices a queenside pawn for lasting pressure on the a- and b-files. The compensation may survive queen exchanges. After the a- and b-pawns open files, Black’s rooks and g7 bishop target White’s queenside.

title: Philidor Defense
body: Black supports e5 with d6 and builds a compact position. The central break must arrive before the pieces become cramped. The d6–e5 chain is stable, but the dark-squared bishop needs a route into the game.

title: Queen's Pawn Game
body: The Colle uses a compact center to prepare e4. Its central break is more important than mechanically repeating a setup. The d4–e3–c3 triangle supports a future e4 but limits the c1 bishop until the center changes.

title: Neo-Grünfeld Defense
body: White delays Nc3 and fianchettoes, avoiding some Exchange Grünfeld structures. Black still seeks pressure against the center. The g2 bishop influences d5; the structure changes sharply after cxd5 or ...dxc4.

body: Featured in The Opera Game, Paris 1858. Morphy exchanges material for development, then uses the open d-file to finish.
